pizzaDough.name: Pizza dough
pizzaDough.summary: Flour, water, salt and yeast or starter for your style and schedule
pizzaDough.knowsWHint: Italian mills print the flour strength (W) on the bag. It decides how long the dough can ferment.

styleDescriptions.neapolitan: Soft, airy rim with charred spots, thin in the middle. Made for a very hot pizza oven.
styleDescriptions.contemporary: Neapolitan with an extra puffy, airy rim from a wetter dough.
styleDescriptions.newYork: Large, thin and foldable with a crisp bottom. A little oil and sugar in the dough.
styleDescriptions.romanTonda: Very thin and crisp, almost like a cracker. Rolled out with a pin.
styleDescriptions.pinsa: Oval, crisp outside and airy inside. Wheat with rice and soy flour in a very wet dough.
styleDescriptions.romanTeglia: Roman pan pizza: a very wet dough with big holes and a crisp bottom. Sold by the slice.
styleDescriptions.detroit: Thick and airy from a deep rectangular pan, with crispy caramelised cheese at the edges.
styleDescriptions.sicilian: Thick, soft and spongy like focaccia, baked in an oiled pan.
styleDescriptions.blechpizza: The home classic: one big pizza on the oven tray.
styleDescriptions.focaccia: Dimpled flatbread with plenty of olive oil, a crisp bottom and a soft crumb.

pizzaDough.ovenInfo: How long a pizza bakes depends on how hot the oven gets and what the pizza lies on. A stone or steel holds heat and bakes the bottom faster than a tray.

ovenDescriptions.tray: The tray that came with the oven.
ovenDescriptions.stone: A stone slab that soaks up heat and gives a crisper bottom.
ovenDescriptions.steel: A steel plate that passes on heat faster than stone, so the pizza is done sooner.
ovenDescriptions.pizzaOven: A gas or wood-fired oven that gets far hotter than a home oven.

ovenTips.tray: Heat the tray upside down with the oven, on the middle rack, and slide the pizza onto it.
ovenTips.stone: Put the stone into the cold oven on the lower or middle rack and heat it at the highest setting for 30 to 60 minutes, thicker stones longer.
ovenTips.steel: Heat the steel with the oven for 30 to 60 minutes on the lower or middle rack. If the top stays pale, finish it under the grill.
ovenTips.pizzaOven: Heat it for 20 to 30 minutes until the stone is hot, measured with an infrared thermometer, and turn the pizza every 20 to 30 seconds.
ovenTips.pan: Start the pan on the lowest rack so the bottom turns crisp.

pizzaDough.ovenMaxInfo: The highest temperature your oven can be set to with top and bottom heat. Most home ovens go up to 250 to 280 °C (480 to 535 °F).
pizzaDough.madeForPizzaOven: {{style}} is usually baked in a pizza oven at about {{temperature}}. Your oven reaches {{max}}, so the pizza needs longer; the time is the one for {{surface}}.
pizzaDough.madeForHotterOven: {{style}} is usually baked at about {{temperature}}; at {{max}} it needs longer. The time is the one for your oven's temperature.
pizzaDough.waterForFlour: {{flour}} takes {{direction}} water than the style's usual flour: the dough gets {{percent}} % instead of {{stylePercent}} %. Hold some water back and add it by feel.

bread.name: Bread & sourdough
bread.summary: Sourdough, rye or yeast bread with ingredients, sour, soaker, schedule and method
bread.flourMixHint: The shares add up to 100 %; the water is set from what each flour takes.
bread.hydrationInfo: Bakers give the water as a percentage of the flour: 63 % means 63 g of water for 100 g of flour. German recipes often give the dough yield instead, Teigausbeute or TA: the weight of dough from 100 g of flour. TA 163 is the same as 63 % water. The higher it is, the softer the dough.
bread.hydrationHint: In % of the flour; dough yield (TA) {{yield}}.
bread.additionsHint: They count towards the loaf's weight, so more of them means less flour. The dough takes their water: all of quark's or eggs', what fruit and vegetables release, far more when cooked or puréed. Seeds and grains go into a soaker.
bread.searchFailed: The food catalogue could not be reached.
bread.waterGiven: {{percent}} % water; the dough takes {{grams}} g per 100 g
bread.waterBound: {{percent}} % water; its starch binds {{grams}} g of the dough's water per 100 g
bread.soaks: Soaks up {{grams, number}} g water per gram
bread.sourTitle: The day before: make the sour
bread.recommendedHydration: The calculator uses {{percent}} % water (dough yield {{yield}}), as is usual for this flour mix.
bread.flourMaxShare: Use it for at most {{share}} % of the flour.

methodDescriptions.starter: Ripe starter goes straight into the dough. Most wheat and spelt sourdough loaves are made this way.
methodDescriptions.sour: Part of the rye ripens the day before with a little starter into a sour, which then goes into the dough whole. Rye needs this acid to bake.
methodDescriptions.yeast: Raised with baker's yeast only, no sourdough.

bread.sourNeedsRye: With rye in the flour you can also make a rye sour the day before.
bread.withYeastHint: Yeast makes up what the sourdough lacks for your schedule, so the dough rises faster and more reliably.
bread.starterPercentHint: In % of the flour. The yeast makes up what it lacks for the schedule.

inDough.sour: All of the sour from the day before

steps.sour: The day before, make the sour: stir the starter into the water, mix in the rye flour and leave it covered to ripen. The next day all of the sour goes into the dough.
steps.soaker: The day before, pour the soaker's water over the seeds and leave them covered to soak.
steps.mixRye: Mix all the ingredients only until the dough is even. Rye dough is not kneaded and stays sticky.
steps.knead: Knead all the ingredients for {{minutes, number}} min, until the dough is smooth and comes away from the bowl.
steps.fold: Leave it covered to rise, and stretch and fold it {{count, number}} times, 30 min apart: pull up one side of the dough, lay it over the middle, and so on all around.
steps.rise: Leave it covered to rise, as in the schedule.
steps.bake: Preheat the oven with a tray or pot to {{start}}, top and bottom heat. Score the loaf and bake it with steam: a dish of water on the oven floor, or with the lid on the pot. After {{after, number}} min, turn it down to {{lower}}; about {{minutes, number}} min in all.
steps.done: It is done at about {{core}} in the middle, or when it sounds hollow as you tap its base. Let it cool on a rack before you cut it.
steps.doneRye: It is done at about {{core}} in the middle, or when it sounds hollow as you tap its base. Let it cool completely on a rack before you cut it: rye bread keeps setting as it cools.
steps.shape_one: About {{hours, number}} h before baking, shape a loaf, lay it seam up in a floured proofing basket or in a loaf tin, and leave it covered to finish rising.
steps.shape_other: About {{hours, number}} h before baking, divide the dough into {{count, number}} equal pieces and shape them into loaves, lay each seam up in a floured proofing basket or loaf tin, and leave them covered to finish rising.

bread.sourHoursHint: The longer it may ripen, the less starter it needs.
bread.sourRiseHint: Without yeast the sour raises the dough: less time needs more sour. Between {{low, number}} and {{high, number}} h the acid stays as rye needs it. For another schedule, add a little yeast.

dough.temperaturesHint: For the water temperature that brings the dough to the temperature it should have.

warnings.flourTooWeakForTime: This flour is made for shorter fermentation than this schedule. Choose a stronger flour or a shorter schedule.
warnings.tooLittleToWeigh: That is less than 0.1 g of yeast, below what kitchen scales weigh.
warnings.impossibleSchedule: No amount of leavener makes this schedule: it is too short or too cold.
warnings.soakerTooLarge: The soaker is more than the dough can carry. Use fewer seeds or more flour.
warnings.additionsTooWet: The additions bring more water than this flour takes, so the dough comes out wetter than the recipe aims for. Use less of them, more flour, or grate them instead of puréeing.
warnings.tooMuchYeast: Far more yeast than usual: the dough tastes of yeast and has no time to develop flavour. Choose a longer schedule.
warnings.moreYeastThanStyleAllows: More yeast than the Neapolitan rules allow (0.1 to 3 g fresh yeast per litre of water). Choose a longer schedule.
warnings.waterTooHot: The water would have to be hotter than 45 °C, which starts to kill yeast. Let the flour warm up, or let the dough rise warmer.
warnings.waterTooCold: The water would have to be colder than ice water. Chill the flour, or knead by hand, which warms the dough less.
warnings.tooManyAdditions: More fruit or vegetables than flour: the crumb may not set and stay gummy.
warnings.ryeWithoutSour: With more than half rye it becomes a rye bread, and rye needs acid. Choose a rye sour the day before.
warnings.flourShareTooHigh: A flour with little or no gluten makes up more of the mix than usual (barley at most a quarter to half, buckwheat, millet, quinoa, amaranth and teff at most half): the loaf turns out dense and crumbly.
warnings.yeastNotNeeded: The sourdough alone raises the dough in this time, so it needs no yeast. Choose a shorter schedule for the yeast to help, or leave it out.

dough.roomInfo: Where the dough rises, usually your kitchen. The flour counts as just as warm, as it is stored there.
dough.temperaturesInfo: Kneading warms the dough by friction, a stand mixer more than hands. The water temperature allows for it, for the room and for the flour.

coffee.name: Coffee
coffee.summary: Coffee and water for filter, French press, espresso, bean-to-cup machines, cold brew and more, with grind, taste profile and steps
coffee.strengthInfo: How much water goes with each gram of coffee, within the usual range for the method. Next to it: how strong the flavour profile judges the coffee to be.

methodDescriptions.pourOver: Hot water poured by hand over ground coffee in a paper filter.
methodDescriptions.filterMachine: A machine drips the hot water through the filter into a jug.
methodDescriptions.frenchPress: The coffee steeps in the water, then a metal sieve presses it down.
methodDescriptions.aeroPress: A plastic tube: a short steep, then pressed through a small paper filter.
methodDescriptions.moka: A stovetop pot: steam pushes the water up through the coffee.
methodDescriptions.espresso: A machine presses hot water through finely ground coffee.
methodDescriptions.coldBrewConcentrate: Steeped cold for hours, then diluted to drink.
methodDescriptions.coldBrewReady: Steeped cold for hours, ready to drink.
methodDescriptions.fullyAutomatic: Grinds the beans and brews at the press of a button, with levels for strength and temperature.

coffee.beansInfo: Dark roasts give up their flavour at cooler water, light roasts need it hotter. Water too cool dissolves too little and the coffee tastes sour; too hot dissolves too much and it turns bitter.

taste.title: Taste
taste.extractionInfo: How much of the ground coffee dissolves in the water. Brewing standards aim for 18 to 22 %: below, coffee tastes sour and thin; above, bitter and dry. It is measured with a refractometer; CookPal estimates it from grind, water temperature, brew time and roast, after measurements.
taste.legend: Like a brewing control chart: to the right, more dissolves from the grounds (extraction); upwards, the drink gets stronger (TDS, the dissolved solids in the drink). Each line is one ratio of coffee to water, and more coffee makes it steeper. Grind, water temperature, brew time, roast and method move your coffee along its line. The green field is balanced, as brewing standards recommend. All values are estimates, not measurements.

coldBrewNote.fridge: In the fridge cold brew dissolves slowly: after the usual 12 to 18 hours it tastes milder, and it is fully extracted only after a good day.
coldBrewNote.room: At room temperature cold brew is fully extracted after about 10 hours; steeping longer hardly changes its strength.

taste.coldExtractionInfo: How much of the grounds dissolves in the water. Cold, it rises slowly and, as measured, stops at 18 to 22 %: after about 10 hours at room temperature, after a good day in the fridge. Steeped shorter, cold brew tastes sweeter and flatter; steeped longer, fuller and harsher. Light roasts give up a little more in the cold than dark ones. CookPal estimates it from these measurements, the time, the place, the roast and the grind.
taste.strongByDesign: The recommended settings already come out a little stronger here than brewing standards call balanced. Less coffee or more water takes you into the green field.

automat.title: Your bean-to-cup machine
automat.hint: Every machine grinds and brews a little differently. CookPal assumes 6 to 12 g of coffee by strength level and 90 to 95 °C: take the result as a direction, not a measurement.
automat.espressoHint: A fully automatic machine usually grinds less coffee per cup than a portafilter and runs more water through it, so its espresso often comes out thinner. A higher level, a smaller cup or two grinds for one cup (such as a double shot), if your machine offers it, make it stronger.
automat.cupHint: The machine grinds the same amount of coffee per level, whatever the cup size: more water makes it thinner. For large cups, many machines offer a double brew with two grinds.

coffee.grindHint: Recommended: {{grind}}. Finer dissolves more from the coffee, coarser less.
coffee.machineWater: For this roast: {{range}}. Set it if your machine allows.
coffee.brewTimeHint: Usual: {{range}}; longer dissolves more, until it hardly grows.

pourOver: Rinse the paper filter with hot water and pour the water away.
Put {{coffee}} of coffee, ground {{grind}}, into the filter.
Pour on {{bloom}} of water at {{temperature}} and let it bloom for 30 to 45 seconds.
Pour the rest in slow circles until {{water}} is in; after about {{time}} it has all run through.
If it runs through faster, grind finer; if it takes longer, coarser.
filterMachine: Fill the tank with {{water}} of water.
Put in a paper filter and {{coffee}} of coffee, ground {{grind}}.
Switch the machine on and let it run through.
frenchPress: Put {{coffee}} of coffee, ground {{grind}}, into the press.
Let it steep for {{time}}, then break the crust with a spoon and skim off the foam and floating bits.
Let it settle for a few minutes, press the plunger only to the surface and pour carefully.
Serve straight away: left in the press it keeps steeping and turns bitter.
aeroPress: Pour on {{water}} of water at {{temperature}} and stir for 10 seconds.
Put on the plunger and, after about {{time}} in all, press gently for 20 to 30 seconds.
moka: Fill the base with water to just below the valve.
Fill the funnel with {{coffee}} of coffee, ground {{grind}}, without pressing it down.
Heat on medium and take it off the heat as soon as no more coffee flows.
espresso: Grind {{coffee}} of coffee {{grind}}, spread it evenly in the portafilter and tamp it level.
Start the shot and stop it after about {{time}} at {{water}} in the cup.
If it runs faster, grind finer; if slower, coarser.
fullyAutomatic: Set the strength, cup size and temperature.
Change the grind only while the grinder runs: standing still, it can be damaged.
If the coffee only drips, grind coarser; if it runs fast and watery, finer.
For dark roasts, lower the temperature by one level.
coldBrewConcentrate: Grind {{coffee}} of coffee {{grind}} and stir it into {{water}} of cold water.
Cover and let it steep {{place}} for about {{time}}.
Strain through a sieve lined with a paper filter, without pressing.
Dilute with {{dilution}} of water before drinking. In the fridge the concentrate keeps about two weeks.
coldBrewReady: Grind {{coffee}} of coffee {{grind}} and stir it into {{water}} of cold water.
Cover and let it steep {{place}} for about {{time}}.
Strain through a sieve lined with a paper filter, without pressing.
In the fridge it keeps about a week.
japaneseIced: Put {{ice}} of ice into the carafe.
Put {{coffee}} of coffee, ground {{grind}}, into the filter, pour on {{bloom}} of hot water at {{temperature}} and let it bloom for 30 to 45 seconds.
Pour on the rest of the hot water until {{water}} is in, and let it run through.
Swirl the carafe until the ice has melted.

methodHints.hot: Steeped the usual way, in hot water.
methodHints.coldBrew: Steeped in cold water for hours in the fridge: milder and hardly bitter.

tea.strengthHint: How much tea goes on the water: more leaves, more of everything.
tea.inTheFridge: About {{hours, number}} h in the fridge
tea.amountAndTimeInfo: Amount and steeping time work differently. The amount sets how concentrated the whole cup is: more leaves give more of everything, in the same balance. The time changes the balance: caffeine, aroma and the sweet amino acids dissolve in the first one to three minutes, tannins keep coming until about six to eight minutes. Steeped briefly, tea tastes fresh and light; longer, fuller and more astringent; after that only more bitter. Herbal and fruit teas have few tannins: there, longer mostly means stronger.
tea.steepTimeHint: Shorter: fresher and lighter. Longer: fuller and more astringent, past the recommendation only more bitter.
tea.steepTimeHintHerbs: Shorter: milder. Longer: stronger in flavour.
tea.infusionsInfo: Good tea leaves can be steeped more than once, these about {{count}} times. As they give less each time, steep each further infusion about {{seconds}} seconds longer than the one before. When it tastes thin, the leaves are spent.
tea.rawHerbsWarning: Herbs, fruit and rooibos are only dried, not heated, and can carry germs that only boiling water kills. Consumer advice is therefore to pour on boiling water, steep at least 5 minutes and then let it cool. Cold brew only teas sold for cold brewing.
